items.q: By the time the rescue team (A) reaches the cave last night, the trapped hikers (B) had already found (C) a narrow passage (D) leading to the surface.
items.explanation: Last night fixes the time in the past, so the verb after by the time must be past simple: reached, with the past perfect for the earlier action.

items.q: Each of the paintings (A) hanging in the school hall (B) were created by students (C) who attend the art club (D) on Saturday mornings.
items.explanation: Each of + plural noun is a singular subject, so it needs a singular verb: was created.

items.q: During our trip to Hue, we hired (A) a local guide who spoke (B) excellent English and knew (C) a history of every (D) royal tomb we visited.
items.explanation: The history is specified by the phrase of every royal tomb, so it takes the definite article: the history of.

items.q: My cousin is (A) extremely good at chemistry, so she (B) has been helping me (C) prepare for the test (D) in Friday.
items.explanation: Days of the week take on: on Friday. In is used for months, years and longer periods.

items.q: The (A) succeed of the school football team this season (B) depends largely on (C) how well the new goalkeeper (D) performs under pressure.
items.explanation: After the and before of we need a noun, not a verb: success.

items.q: Tom and (A) his brother argued about (B) who bicycle had been left in the rain, but (C) neither of them (D) admitted the mistake.
items.explanation: Possession before a noun needs the possessive form whose; who cannot stand directly in front of bicycle.

items.q: The weather in the mountains this week (A) has been (B) far colder (C) as the forecast predicted, so (D) most climbers stayed in the lodge.
items.explanation: A comparative adjective (colder) is followed by than, not as; as only pairs with as … as.

items.q: If the volcano (A) erupts again this year, thousands of villagers (B) will have to leave (C) their homes and (D) would move to temporary shelters.
items.explanation: This is a first conditional (if + present, will); the second verb shares will have to, so would mixes in the second conditional wrongly.

items.q: The tour guide told us (A) that we didn't touch the ancient carvings because (B) the oils on our hands (C) could damage (D) the stone over time.
items.explanation: A reported instruction uses tell + object + (not) to + verb: told us not to touch, not a that-clause with a past tense.

items.q: The scientist (A) who discovered the new species of frog, (B) that lives only in one cave, (C) named it after (D) her old teacher.
options: that lives only in one cave
items.correction: which lives only in one cave
items.explanation: A non-defining relative clause (between commas) cannot begin with that; for a thing or animal use which.

items.q: Although the museum (A) is open every day, (B) my parents want to know (C) when does it close so we (D) can plan the afternoon.
items.explanation: In an indirect question after want to know, the word order is statement order with no auxiliary does: when it closes.

items.q: Before the exam started, the teacher reminded everyone (A) to switch off their phones, (B) to read every question carefully and (C) to avoid (D) doing careless mistakes.
items.explanation: The verb that collocates with mistake is make, never do: make a mistake.

items.q: (A) A few of the furniture in the old library (B) was donated by families (C) whose children had studied there (D) many decades ago.
items.explanation: Furniture is uncountable, so a few (for plural countables) is impossible; use some or a little.

items.q: The farmers (A) planted the rice early this year (B) despite the rains came late, (C) which meant the young plants (D) had to be watered by hand.
options: had to be watered by hand
items.explanation: Despite is a preposition and takes a noun phrase; a full clause with subject and verb needs the conjunction although.

items.q: When I (A) phoned my grandfather yesterday evening, he (B) said that he (C) is watching a documentary about (D) penguins in Antarctica.
items.explanation: After a past reporting verb (said) the present continuous shifts back to the past continuous: was watching.

items.q: Neither the coach (A) nor the players (B) were surprised when the referee (C) stopped the match because the lights (D) was failing.
items.explanation: The subject the lights is plural, so the verb must be plural: were failing. (B) is correct because with neither … nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject, the players.

items.q: (A) Kite made by my grandfather (B) flew higher than any of the ones (C) sold in the market, (D) although it looked rather plain.
items.correction: The kite made by my grandfather
items.explanation: A singular countable noun cannot stand alone; because it is identified by made by my grandfather, it needs the.

items.q: The new bridge (A) across the river will be (B) finished by the end from March, (C) which means the ferry (D) will stop running.
options: finished by the end from March
items.correction: finished by the end of March
items.explanation: The fixed phrase is at/by the end of a period: the end of March.

items.q: Bees are (A) surprisingly clever insects that (B) can remember (C) the exactly position of a flower (D) several kilometres from their hive.
items.explanation: A noun (position) is described by an adjective, not an adverb: exact, not exactly.

items.q: My sister and I (A) baked a chocolate cake for our mother's birthday, but the dog (B) got into the kitchen and (C) ate half of (D) them.
items.explanation: The pronoun refers back to a chocolate cake, which is singular, so it must be it, not them.

items.q: This year's science fair was (A) the more crowded event the school (B) has ever organised, with (C) nearly two hundred projects (D) on display.
items.explanation: The … ever compares one event with all the others, so the superlative is needed: the most crowded.

items.q: If people (A) in the city (B) will cycle to work instead of driving, the air (C) would be cleaner and the streets (D) much quieter.
items.explanation: The result clause uses would, so this is a second conditional and the if-clause takes the past simple: if people cycled.

items.q: The astronaut (A) explained to the children that the Earth (B) looks blue from space and (C) asked them if had they ever seen (D) a picture of it.
options: asked them if had they ever seen
items.correction: asked them if they had ever seen
items.explanation: A reported yes/no question keeps statement word order after if: if they had ever seen, with no inversion.

items.q: Our history teacher, (A) whose lessons are never boring, (B) took us to (C) a small museum (D) where it displays letters from the war.
options: where it displays letters from the war
items.correction: which displays letters from the war
items.explanation: Where is a relative adverb and cannot be the subject of displays; the clause needs the relative pronoun which as its subject.

items.q: (A) My aunt speaks very well Japanese because she (B) spent six years (C) working for a car company (D) outside Tokyo.
options: My aunt speaks very well Japanese
items.correction: My aunt speaks Japanese very well
items.explanation: An adverb of manner does not come between a verb and its object; the order is verb + object + adverb: speaks Japanese very well.

items.q: While we were waiting for the bus, my friend (A) asked a stranger (B) to make a photo of us (C) in front of (D) the old clock tower.
options: to make a photo of us
items.correction: to take a photo of us
items.explanation: In English you take a photo; make a photo is not a natural collocation.

items.q: The library (A) has plenty of books about space, but (B) there are (C) very little magazines (D) on the subject.
items.explanation: Magazines is a plural countable noun, so the quantifier is few; little goes only with uncountable nouns.

items.q: The ferry (A) to the island (B) was delayed (C) for three hours (D) because the thick fog over the harbour.
items.explanation: Because must introduce a clause with a verb; before a noun phrase (the thick fog) use because of.

items.q: Scientists (A) have found the wreck of the ship in 2019, (B) almost a century after (C) it sank (D) during a winter storm.
items.explanation: A finished time expression (in 2019) requires the past simple; the present perfect cannot be used with a specific past date.

items.q: My father (A) gave up (B) to smoke last year and (C) now spends the money (D) on trips with the family.
items.explanation: The phrasal verb give up is followed by a gerund, not an infinitive: gave up smoking.

items.q: We spent (A) a wonderful week in Sapa, but (B) the hotel was (C) at top of a steep hill, (D) which was tiring.
options: at top of a steep hill
items.correction: at the top of a steep hill
items.explanation: The fixed phrase is at the top of; the definite article cannot be dropped before top.

items.q: The doctor (A) is responsible of the health of over three hundred patients (B) in the village, (C) so she (D) rarely takes a day off.
items.explanation: The adjective responsible takes the preposition for: responsible for the health.

items.q: The city council (A) has decided to (B) wide the main road (C) so that buses (D) can run more frequently during rush hour.
items.explanation: After decided to a verb is needed; wide is an adjective and its verb form is widen.

items.q: After the concert, (A) the conductor came over and (B) thanked (C) my sister and I for (D) helping to set up the chairs.
options: helping to set up the chairs
items.explanation: The pronoun is the object of thanked, so the object form me is required; I is only a subject.

items.q: The new stadium (A) holds twice (B) as many people (C) as the old one, but (D) the seats are not as comfortable than before.
options: the seats are not as comfortable than before
items.correction: the seats are not as comfortable as before
items.explanation: An equal comparison is (not) as + adjective + as; than belongs only with a comparative form like more comfortable.

items.q: If our school (A) had a swimming pool, (B) more students (C) will join the swimming team (D) instead of travelling across town.
items.explanation: The if-clause is in the past simple (had), which is a second conditional, so the result clause takes would, not will.

items.q: When I met Minh last week, he (A) told me that his family (B) was moving to Can Tho (C) the following month and that he (D) will miss his friends here.
items.explanation: After a past reporting verb (told), will shifts back to would, just as are moving became was moving.

items.q: The girl (A) which won the poetry competition (B) is only twelve, but her poem (C) about the river (D) made several judges cry.
items.explanation: Which refers to things; for a person the relative pronoun is who (or that).

items.q: Lan (A) is a careful student who (B) always is the first to finish (C) her homework and (D) never forgets to check it.
items.explanation: An adverb of frequency goes after the verb be but before other verbs: is always, yet never forgets.

items.q: The strong wind last night (A) blew several tiles off the roof, and (B) my father (C) had to (D) do an urgent phone call to a builder.
options: blew several tiles off the roof
items.explanation: The collocation is make a phone call; do is used for tasks and activities, not for calls.
